title: Quoting and changing
hookLine: he kept adding to the Essays in the margins until he died

cards: Open a secondhand book and sometimes there's a stranger in it: pencil in the margins, a word underlined, a question mark, a date, a small argument with the author.

Tradition says Montaigne did something like that to his own book. Once the Essays were printed and out in the world, he kept adding to them: new sentences, new quotations, second thoughts that didn't erase the first ones.
Today, a book that never quite stopped being written, and the man who said why.

teach.h: I ADD, BUT I DON'T CORRECT.
teach.b: First, his rule. In the essay Of vanity, Montaigne says it plainly: I add, but I don't correct. Once the book had gone out, he felt it belonged partly to its readers.
And he wasn't sure his later self was wiser than his earlier one.

teach.h: MYSELF NOW AND THEN ARE TWO.
teach.b: Myself now and myself a while ago, he says, are indeed two. So the old self keeps its say, and the new self adds a note beside it. Second, the quoting.
His pages are full of other people's words, many of them in Latin.
In the essay Of books he explains: he makes others say what he can't say so well himself. Third, his trick. Sometimes, he admits, he leaves the author's name off on purpose.
That way a critic who sneers at the line, thinking it's his, ends up flicking Plutarch on the nose, or burning his fingers insulting Seneca. Fourth, what this makes the book.

teach.h: A NOTE BESIDE THE OLD PAGE.
teach.b: Not a monument but a conversation: his voice and the old voices, his younger thoughts and his older ones, all left standing on the same page.
Your life has old pages too: a letter, a journal, an opinion you once held loudly. You don't have to tear them out. You can write beside them.

how: Montaigne says in the essay Of vanity that he adds to his book but does not correct it, and in Of books that he borrows other writers' words to say what he cannot say as well.

o: filling his book with others' words and adding, not erasing
copying out old books by hand to sell in his town
rewriting each essay until no first version was left

games.q: inside quoting and changing: tap the pairs.
p: I add, but I don't correct
myself now and a while ago
say what he can't say so well

s: Montaigne rewrote his book to fix what he'd said before
he says he adds but doesn't correct.
he sometimes left an author's name off a quotation on purpose
so a sneering critic would end up insulting Seneca or Plutarch.
he thought his later self was surely wiser
he wasn't sure, and said his present and past selves were two.

games.q: your book is printed and out in the world. you've changed your mind about a page. what does Montaigne do?
o: cross it out and rewrite it.
add a new thought beside it and leave the old one standing.
games.why: I add, but I don't correct. the old self keeps its say; the new self writes beside it.

practice: Bring to mind something you once said, wrote or firmly believed a few years back, and let that younger self have their say without judging them.
Then, quietly, add one line beside it, the way Montaigne added to his own pages: not a correction, just what you'd add now.

wordCard.voice: Quoting and changing. Montaigne filled his book with other people's words and kept adding his own, without crossing out what he'd said before. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: keep adding. Myself now and myself a while ago both get a say. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Essays 3.9, Of vanity (he adds but does not correct; himself now and himself a while ago are two)
Essays 2.10, Of books (he makes others say what he cannot say so well; names left off so critics strike Plutarch or Seneca)
